pages.title: Microsoft’s MacBook Pro Rival Is Looking Even More Ridiculous
pages.text:
Microsoft’s MacBook Pro Rival Is Looking Even More Ridiculous
We thought Microsoft was preparing a wild laptop. Turns out it's preparing two.
The Surface Laptop Ultra may bring a new class of machine to the Windows space. © Kyle Barr / Gizmodo
At this point, the writing has been on the wall for Microsoft’s Surface Laptop Ultra for some time. The company has been parading the thing around all summer, heralding its AI capabilities and demonstrating its capacity to chew through demanding games with admirable ease. We’ve known since Computex that the Ultra would be among a whole laundry list of laptops rolling out this year powered by Nvidia’s new RTX Spark, an Apple-style superchip that staples a CPU, GPU, and unified memory together. And that, along with Microsoft’s not-at-all-subtle marketing, made it fairly evident that the Surface Laptop Ultra was being positioned as an AI machine.
Here’s where things get interesting. The RTX Spark platform has two variants: one with 18 cores and one with 20. We predicted back at IFA that many laptops would contain the 18-core chip, given that that’s, you know, the one that seems more evidently useful for laptops and that Nvidia was demoing the 20-core version in mini PCs at the same show.
But the Surface Laptop Ultra, it turns out, is not trying to be an ordinary laptop. Windows Central’s Zac Bowden has leaked nearly all remaining details of Microsoft’s upcoming MacBook Pro competitor, and one of them is very spicy. Per the leaks, Microsoft will be selling the Ultra with both RTX Spark variants, including that 20-core monstrosity that we all kind of figured we’d only see crammed into weird-looking mini PCs.
Microsoft’s eighteener reportedly maxes out at 32GB of memory; the 20-core guy goes all the way up to 128GB. Also of note: the entry-level 18-core SKUs will reportedly run Windows 11 Home, while higher-end configs get Windows 11 Pro. The tangible difference between these operating systems is mainly security and virtualization stuff, but the signaling here is important—the 20-core option is targeting a very different market segment.
The Surface Laptop (above) could be morphing into a laptop that rivals the most powerful MacBook Pro. © Kyle Barr / Gizmodo
This is interesting for a few reasons. The fact that Microsoft is positioning this Ultra device as a rival to Apple’s M5 Max MacBook Pro is no secret (I mean, look at the thing). What I didn’t necessarily expect was that Redmond planned on spanning the whole gamut, from the 24GB entry-level notebook all the way up the chain.
Bowden’s sources say that the upcoming event will focus on “how Surface Laptop Ultra and RTX Spark are capable of running local 120B parameter models that enable on-device AI experiences and agentic workflows,” and that the company plans to “demonstrate how the Surface Laptop Ultra maintains maximum performance even when not plugged in.” These both appear to be direct attacks on what Apple’s most premium systems are traditionally known for in this space: maintaining high performance on battery and enabling large local AI workloads to dive headfirst into a massive pool of memory.
Previously, there was a real question as to whether Microsoft was building one several-thousand-dollar halo product tailored to folks who know what “120B parameter model” means or a broader product family. Now, we at least know that there are two clear tiers. Microsoft has one horse in the premium consumer laptop race and another that’s just hoping to take a big bite out of the customer base Apple’s arguably had cornered since the launch of the M-series. It’s shoving the maximum possible performance into a machine with a 2,000-nit-peak-HDR screen and hoping for the best.
Of course, this whole equation is missing one major variable: cost. Bowden’s sources have not confirmed an exact price, and that number will definitively determine where this 20-core Ultra model fits in the current market. I’m willing to make a bold prediction, though: it probably won’t be cheap.

pages.title: Is Outlook Down? Users Report Possible Microsoft Outlook Problems, Weeks After Multi-Day Exchange Outage
pages.text:
Is Outlook Down? Users Report Possible Microsoft Outlook Problems, Weeks After Multi-Day Exchange Outage
REDMOND, Wash. — Users reported possible problems with Microsoft Outlook on Monday, according to the outage-tracking service Downdetector, though the sources reviewed for this article did not show a confirmed Microsoft statement about an incident today. The reports come weeks after one of the most disruptive email outages of the year for Microsoft 365 customers.
Downdetector flagged a rise in user reports about Outlook, Microsoft's email and calendar application, which is offered on the web, PC, Mac and mobile as part of Microsoft 365 and provides messaging, scheduling, contact management and task organization. The alert provided did not include the number of reports, the regions affected or the specific symptoms. Downdetector's figures reflect user-submitted complaints rather than a verified count of affected customers, and a spike can have causes that are local to a network, an organization or a device. Microsoft had not, in the coverage reviewed, acknowledged a new problem or offered an explanation.
Users who suspect an outage can check Microsoft's own status channels. Administrators should look first at the Service Health section of the Microsoft 365 admin center, and the public service status page and the Microsoft 365 Status account on X provide a broader view, according to a guide from the security firm Hornetsecurity. "Third-party tools, such as Downdetector, can help you determine if other users are already experiencing similar issues," the firm wrote. "However, they should not replace checking your organization's service status." Basic steps that outlets have suggested during past disruptions include refreshing Outlook, restarting the app, checking the internet connection and trying Outlook on the web.
The recent history explains why users are sensitive to any sign of trouble. On August 31, Microsoft began investigating an Exchange Online incident tracked as EX1464935, which produced delays and failures in sending and receiving email, authentication errors and problems with mailbox search, according to Microsoft's advisory as reported by Hornetsecurity. "We've confirmed that users may experience degraded functionality with various Exchange Online functionalities," Microsoft's status account wrote on X. "We're reviewing service telemetry and diagnostic data to isolate the source of the issue."
Microsoft later attributed the problem to authentication. A preliminary root cause published in the incident updates described "an issue within a core authentication configuration used by multiple Microsoft 365 services," according to Tom's Guide's live coverage. BleepingComputer reported that Microsoft began tracking a broader incident, MO1465074, which also affected Teams, Microsoft Graph, Purview, OneDrive for Business, SharePoint Online, the Microsoft 365 admin center, Copilot, Universal Print and Defender XDR. In an update reproduced by TechCrunch, Microsoft said it had identified an issue with an "authentication component" and was testing a remediation on part of its infrastructure.
The disruption lasted more than a day. TechCrunch reported on September 1 that Microsoft's effort to fix what had become a multi-day outage was entering its second day, and that as of Tuesday the issues were not fully resolved. In a status update that day, Microsoft said, "Indications from telemetry remain positive, and we've confirmed service availability is improving," adding that it was entering a period of extended monitoring. By September 2, Microsoft reported considerable recovery even though some users still faced problems, according to a report by The Sunday Guardian. GV Wire reported that more than 6,000 users reported problems on Downdetector on Wednesday, September 2, and that Monday's outage had drawn reports from more than 50,000 users. The Sunday Guardian cited more than 130,000 Downdetector reports for the incident, a figure it said should not be read as an exact count of affected customers.
The August incident followed other disruptions this year. On January 22, a Microsoft 365 outage lasting nearly 10 hours affected services including Outlook, Defender and Purview, The Register reported, with Microsoft blaming "a portion of service infrastructure in North America that is not processing traffic as expected." Downdetector reports peaked at about 15,000 or more that day, and Microsoft confirmed early on January 23 that the impact had been resolved, according to reporting syndicated on Yahoo. Cybersecurity News noted earlier this year that Microsoft traced an Exchange Online incident, EX1454755, to a DNS-related fault at a third-party email provider, and that in June a mail-flow pipeline issue caused delivery delays across North America, Europe and Asia-Pacific, with some messages undelivered for more than an hour.
Outlook problems can also be easy to misattribute. Many Microsoft 365 subscribers connect through Exchange Online, Microsoft's cloud email platform, which means a fault in that service can look like an Outlook problem even if the application itself is unchanged, The Sunday Guardian explained. That distinction matters for administrators, who use different incident numbers for Exchange-specific and broader Microsoft 365 issues.
Whether Monday's reports reflect a genuine platform incident is not yet clear from the information available. Outage trackers can register spikes when a single company's network fails or when a popular service has a brief glitch, and Downdetector's own description of the current alert uses the phrase "possible problems." Microsoft's status channels are the authoritative place to look for confirmation. If a service incident is declared, the company typically posts an incident number in the admin center and updates through X.
For readers affected now, the practical advice is to check the Microsoft 365 Status account and the admin center before troubleshooting further, to try Outlook on the web if the desktop or mobile app will not sync, and to expect that any backlog of delayed messages may take time to clear if a broader outage is confirmed. This article will be updated if Microsoft acknowledges an incident.

pages.title: Dear Microsoft Stock Fans, Mark Your Calendars for October 7

Dear Microsoft Stock Fans, Mark Your Calendars for October 7
Tue, October 6, 2026 at 11:55 AM PDT 5 min read
Microsoft France headquarters by JeanLuclchard via Shutterstock
Microsoft's (MSFT) cloud business is booming, but its PC business has ground to recover. In the quarter ended June 30, Azure and other cloud services revenue jumped 43%, helping push total revenue to $90 billion, up 18% from a year earlier. Windows OEM and Devices revenue, however, fell 7%. That contrast makes the next Windows and Surface announcements worth watching for signs of stronger customer demand.
Microsoft will share its latest Windows and Surface news tomorrow, Oct. 7, at 10 a.m. Pacific time. The event is expected to take place in San Francisco, with CEO Satya Nadella, Windows and Devices chief Pavan Davuluri, and Nvidia (NVDA) CEO Jensen Huang discussing local AI. This expected focus includes the RTX Spark platform, Surface hardware, and Windows experiences designed to run AI directly on devices.

Those features could give customers a reason to upgrade, making demand more important to shareholders than hardware specifications alone. Can Microsoft turn that interest into stronger Windows and Surface sales? Let's find out.
Based in Redmond, Washington, Microsoft develops productivity software, operates Azure cloud services, and sells Windows licenses, Surface devices, and gaming products. Its market capitalization stands at approximately $3,843 billion. Beyond hardware, the company serves consumers and enterprises through subscriptions, infrastructure, and AI tools embedded across its expanding portfolio of digital services.
Microsoft shares finished trading on Oct. 5 at $525.18, delivering a year-to-date (YTD) advance of 8.59% and a more modest 1.51% gain over the prior 52 weeks.
The stock trades at 11.47 times sales and 22.76 times cash flow, well above the sector medians of 3.72x and 18.94x. In addition, shareholders are entitled to a forward annual dividend of $3.64 per share, equating to a current yield of 0.71%.
Microsoft Corp. released its fiscal Q4 2026 results on July 29, covering the June quarter, also described as Q2 CY2026. Their revenue rose 17.7% year-over-year (YoY) to $90.01 billion, beating analysts' $87.71 billion estimate by 2.6%.
This sales growth accompanied GAAP EPS of $4.81, exceeding the $4.22 consensus forecast by 14.1%. MSFT maintained a 45.1% operating margin, but its free cash flow margin declined to 21.8% from 33.4%, leaving less cash per revenue dollar after capital spending.
Microsoft generated 41.5% of total revenue through Intelligent Cloud, the segment containing Azure and its AI-related computing services. Their segment revenue increased 31.6% YoY, making cloud demand central to the earnings story.
This business delivered 17.9% annualized growth over five years, faster than Microsoft's consolidated revenue growth. The preceding two years averaged 14.4% annualized growth, making the latest quarterly acceleration particularly notable.
Where Microsoft's AI Growth Could Come From
Nokia (NOK) expanded its Microsoft partnership on Sept. 17 to develop an agentic, unified data foundation for telecommunications providers. The aim is to help operators automate network tasks and run AI-driven operations more reliably. This creates another enterprise use for Microsoft's technology, though neither company disclosed the deal's value or expected revenue.
While that partnership's financial contribution remains unspecified, Copilot offers measurable evidence of customer demand. Its paid user base exceeded 30 million, and net seat additions more than doubled quarter over quarter. Those subscriptions provide a clearer measure of AI adoption than product demonstrations.
Taken together, these developments show where Microsoft can turn AI demand into revenue through enterprise services, paid subscriptions, and higher cloud prices. Windows and Surface offer another opportunity to connect useful AI features with products customers already use.
Microsoft's next earnings release is listed for Nov. 4, with its September-quarter EPS estimates averaging $4.70, versus $4.13 a year earlier, implying 13.80% growth.
Wells Fargo added Microsoft to its Q4 tactical ideas list with an "Overweight" rating and a reported Street-high $725 target. Analyst Michael Turrin sees attractive valuations and several catalysts supporting his outlook. He expects the new reporting structure to clarify how AI investments translate into revenue.
That optimism extends to other firms. Stifel raised its target to $530 from $450 while maintaining "Hold" in one report. Separately, it upgraded MSFT from "Hold" to "Buy" on Sept. 22, arguing that the company had decisively turned a corner.
Overall, 51 surveyed analysts rate MSFT stock a "Strong Buy," though that does not mean every analyst recommends buying. Their average $568.15 target implies 7.77% upside from MSFT's Oct. 5 closing price.
Oct. 7 deserves a spot on Microsoft shareholders' calendars, but expectations should stay grounded. The Windows and Surface event is more likely to strengthen the existing growth story than immediately change Microsoft's earnings outlook. Useful AI features could encourage upgrades, though customer adoption will matter more than impressive demonstrations. With analysts already expecting earnings growth, the announcements need commercial substance to support further optimism.

pages.text:
A $1,000 Bet on Microsoft a Decade Ago Crushed the Market by Over 3x
A single Microsoft investment a decade ago left the S&P 500 in the dust, but the reasons behind those gains reveal something surprising about what actually drove the returns and whether the next decade could come close.
Published October 6, 2026, 3:00pm ET · 2 min read
This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them.
The vibrant display of soaring stock charts and financial data reflects the dynamic growth often seen in successful investments. This visual metaphor underscores the impressive returns discussed in the article regarding long-term holdings. © Travis Wolfe / Shutterstock.com
Ten years ago, buying Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT | MSFT Price Prediction) looked like a safe, slightly sleepy call on Windows and Office. However, it would become one of the best large-cap holdings of the decade. And almost none of that gain came from the dividend.
CEO Satya Nadella spent the decade moving Microsoft away from one-time licenses and toward recurring subscriptions and Azure cloud capacity. Office became Microsoft 365, so customers paid every month instead of once per upgrade cycle. Deals for LinkedIn (2016), GitHub (2018) and Activision Blizzard (2023) strengthened its hold on corporate IT departments and developers.
Then AI arrived, and the OpenAI partnership made Azure a default home for enterprise AI work. In fiscal 2026, Azure exceeded $100 billion in annual revenue for the first time. Microsoft 365 Copilot passed 30 million paid seats. Commercial remaining performance obligations (signed revenue not yet booked) reached $678 billion, up 84%.
Your $1,000 Became $10,384, and the Index Trailed Far Behind
S&P 500 (same period): $1,167.50 (16.75%)
S&P 500 (same period): $1,796.40 (79.64%)
S&P 500 (same period): $3,633.10 (263.31%)
Microsoft’s returns use dividend-adjusted prices. The S&P 500 figures track SPY’s price change. With a yield near 0.68%, income was a rounding error. The quarterly payout rose every year, from $0.36 in 2016 to $0.98. That steady growth matters more than the yield, but price gains did nearly all the work.
Timing made a big difference. The 10-year holder beat the index easily, the 5-year holder beat it narrowly, and the 1-year holder fell behind. Over the past year the stock has traded between $348.54 and $549.20, as investors considered fiscal 2026 capex of $115.95 billion (+79.62%) against free cash flow that fell 6.46%.
What Could Make or Break the Next Decade for Microsoft
The bull case depends on Azure turning its capacity shortage into revenue. Management is guiding for roughly 45% constant-currency Azure growth, and CFO Amy Hood said “demand exceeds available supply.” At about 25 times forward earnings, that growth looks fairly priced. The expansion also lifts a wider circle of suppliers (we analyzed seven of the power, cooling, and networking names behind the AI data-center push in a free report).
The bear case centers on AI spending running ahead of cash flow. Expected capital expenditures of roughly $175 billion only pay off if demand holds. Add rising OpenAI investment losses, regulatory scrutiny and a shrinking PC business, and a disappointment at about 29 times trailing earnings could hurt.
Today’s setup looks very different from 2016. Back then, investors underrated the cloud shift. Today, AI is the consensus story, and the company is worth about $3.96 trillion. The setup supports steady compounding, while another tenfold decade looks far harder to repeat from this starting point.

pages.text:

Microsoft Corporation (US5949181045) zeigt Mitarbeitende im modernen hellen Office mit Monitoren und Videocall-Display, Illustration mit AI erstellt.
Microsoft Corporation stock (ISIN US5949181045) is trading near its recent highs after the software giant reported a strong fiscal fourth quarter in late July, posting revenue of USD 90.01 billion and earnings per share of USD 4.74 that topped Wall Street expectations according to MarketBeat on July 29, 2026. As of the last completed trading day before the Labor Day holiday on September 4, 2026, market data indicate that Microsoft’s share price on Nasdaq was close to its 52-week high, reflecting investor confidence in the company’s AI-driven growth.
In its fiscal fourth quarter ended in late July 2026, Microsoft generated revenue of USD 90.01 billion, exceeding consensus estimates of around USD 87.62 billion reported by MarketBeat. That represents approximately 17.7 percent year-over-year growth for the quarter, highlighting how demand across cloud and productivity products continues to expand. Earnings per share reached USD 4.74 versus a consensus of USD 4.24, meaning Microsoft delivered USD 0.50 EPS above expectations in the quarter, a gap that underscores ongoing operating leverage in its software and cloud businesses.
According to a recent analysis on Yahoo Finance dated September 7, 2026, the July results marked a record fiscal fourth quarter for Microsoft, with Azure revenue surpassing USD 100 billion annually after growing 43 percent during the quarter. That annualized Azure revenue figure, combined with double-digit overall growth, shows how AI workloads are translating into concrete cloud spending and positions Microsoft as a key beneficiary of the latest generative AI cycle. For investors, the notable point is that the company is turning heavy AI infrastructure investments into higher revenue rather than margin pressure, at least in the near term.
The July earnings report triggered a clear reaction in Microsoft stock, with the share price jumping roughly 17 percent in the period following the results as investors rewarded the company’s AI execution, according to Yahoo Finance on September 7, 2026. That move pushed the stock toward the upper end of its recent trading range and close to its 52-week high, signaling that the market now prices in stronger cloud growth and a premium for Microsoft’s strategic positioning in AI. While exact valuation multiples depend on the latest intraday data, this post-earnings rally illustrates how quickly sentiment can shift when a large-cap technology name demonstrates above-consensus growth and clear traction in a key theme such as AI.
At the same time, the broader US equity market has seen periods of volatility around interest rate expectations and inflation data, and Microsoft’s share performance is partly framed by those macro factors. With Azure growth accelerating and the company forecasting substantial capital expenditures for fiscal 2027 in support of AI infrastructure, the stock embodies both opportunity and risk: high growth potential but also sensitivity to any slowdown in enterprise spending or changes in the cost of capital. For long-term shareholders, the balance between sustained double-digit revenue growth and disciplined cost management remains central to the investment case.
Guidance, capex and the next earnings date
Ahead of its next quarterly report, market commentary compiled by TradingKey on September 6, 2026 highlights consensus expectations for Microsoft’s upcoming fiscal quarter: around USD 87.67 billion in revenue and USD 4.24 in EPS for Q4 of fiscal 2026. While those figures are estimates rather than final reported results, they provide a benchmark that investors will use to evaluate whether Microsoft can maintain the strong trajectory seen in the July quarter. In addition, guidance discussed in recent coverage points to fiscal 2027 capital expenditures in the range of USD 255 billion to USD 260 billion, which would represent roughly a 35 percent increase from about USD 190 billion spent in calendar 2026. This step-up in investment underscores how aggressively Microsoft is building out its AI and cloud infrastructure to meet expected demand.
Looking ahead, the next major catalyst for Microsoft stock is its forthcoming earnings release, which market calendars and previews indicate is scheduled for late October 2026, after the close of US trading. The accompanying conference call is expected to start around 5:30 PM Eastern Time on the reporting day, giving investors and analysts the opportunity to assess updated guidance, Azure growth trends and any changes to the company’s capex plans. With the July quarter having delivered both a top-line beat and EPS outperformance, the bar for the next print is higher, and any deviation from the current consensus on growth or margins could quickly impact the share price.
Risks around AI spending and macro conditions
Despite the current strength, several risk factors accompany the bullish narrative around Microsoft stock. One key risk is the sheer scale of planned AI-related capital expenditure: an increase of roughly one-third from calendar 2026 levels implies a heavy upfront investment that must be matched by sustained demand and pricing power in Azure and related services. If enterprise AI adoption were to slow or shift toward lower-margin offerings, the returns on this capex could come under scrutiny, which in turn might weigh on the stock. In addition, intense competition from other hyperscale cloud providers and AI platform companies means Microsoft must continuously innovate to defend its share of high-value workloads.
Macro conditions provide another layer of uncertainty. Analysts and market observers note that upcoming US inflation data and Federal Reserve decisions on interest rates will influence overall risk appetite, including for large-cap technology stocks such as Microsoft. A higher-for-longer interest rate environment tends to pressure valuation multiples for growth stocks, and any surprise in inflation figures could lead to short-term volatility in the share price even if company-specific fundamentals remain strong. For investors, monitoring both Microsoft’s execution on AI and the broader rate backdrop is essential when interpreting the stock’s moves around upcoming earnings dates.
Azure and Microsoft 365 as core products
Within Microsoft’s portfolio, the Azure cloud platform and Microsoft 365 productivity suite stand out as the main drivers of the recent earnings beat. Azure’s reported 43 percent quarterly growth in the latest fiscal quarter and more than USD 100 billion in annualized revenue underscore its central role in the company’s strategy to capture AI-related demand, according to Yahoo Finance. Many new generative AI services, including integrations with OpenAI’s ChatGPT-based models, run on Azure infrastructure, which supports high-margin consumption of compute and storage. The continued expansion of these services is a key reason why investors have rewarded Microsoft stock in the wake of the July earnings.
Microsoft 365, which bundles Office applications with collaboration tools like Teams and security features, contributes recurring subscription revenue that stabilizes the company’s overall earnings profile. As enterprises adopt AI capabilities within productivity software, such as AI copilots embedded in Office applications, these products increasingly link day-to-day usage to Microsoft’s broader AI platform. For shareholders, this combination of fast-growing Azure revenue and steady Microsoft 365 subscription income provides a diversified earnings base supporting the high level of investment in AI infrastructure.
Stock level and market data as of the last trading day
Because US equity markets are closed for Labor Day on September 7, 2026, there is no regular trading session for Microsoft stock on that date, and the most recent official price data come from the prior trading day. According to US market holiday schedules compiled by INDmoney, both the New York Stock Exchange and Nasdaq were fully closed on September 7, with trading set to resume on September 8, 2026. As of the close on September 4, 2026, Microsoft’s share price on Nasdaq stood near the top of its 52-week range, with the 52-week high only a few percent above that closing level and the 52-week low significantly lower, reflecting a strong upward move over the past year. Market capitalization figures from recent stock portal data place Microsoft firmly among the world’s largest listed companies, with a valuation in the trillions of US dollars as of early September 2026.
Daily trading volume in Microsoft shares typically reaches tens of millions of shares on Nasdaq, and the last completed trading day before the holiday period was no exception, with robust liquidity enabling institutional investors to adjust positions in response to the July earnings beat and evolving AI expectations. For retail investors, this deep liquidity and tight bid-ask spreads help reduce transaction costs when entering or exiting positions around key events such as earnings releases and macro data prints. The combination of high liquidity, strong fundamental growth, and a clearly defined AI narrative is a major reason why Microsoft stock continues to occupy a central role in many diversified equity portfolios.

pages.title: Satya Nadella reinvented Microsoft once. Can he do it again in the AI era?
pages.text:
Satya Nadella reinvented Microsoft once. Can he do it in the AI era?
Satya Nadella revived Microsoft after succeeding Steve Ballmer in 2014, turning the company into a cloud powerhouse.
But almost four years into the artificial intelligence boom, the software giant has yet to find a breakout hit at the model or application layer.
Part of Nadella's challenge involves shifting the business model yet again, this time to center it around tokens, the currency of the AI economy.
Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella speaks at the Microsoft AI Tour event in Munich, Germany, on Feb. 25, 2026.
Sven Hoppe | Picture Alliance | Getty Images
On a sunny day in Seattle in late September, about 50 executives representing large Microsoft customers had a rare opportunity. They could ask anything of CEO Satya Nadella.
One attendee wanted to know what Microsoft could do to help companies adapt to the artificial intelligence age. Nadella responded by emphasizing the importance of "diffusion inside the enterprise," meaning AI tools need to be widely deployed.
"Like all things, change is always bottom up, top down, and middle up," said Nadella, sporting a tight black crewneck and dark gray slacks, as he strode across the stage at the downtown Paccar Pavilion.
For the 59-year-old Nadella, who's spent over half his life at Microsoft, the gathering landed at a pivotal moment, as the software giant tries to magnify its role in the AI boom. Of late, Nadella has been inserting himself more into the AI discourse, posting on X last month about the need for "deliberate pacing" in model development, and days later addressing safety fears at the All-In Summit in Los Angeles.
Despite its almost $4 trillion market cap, Microsoft has yet to break out as an AI leader. Nvidia dominates in AI chips, Anthropic and OpenAI boast the foremost models, Meta just released the first mass-market personal agent, and Google's Gemini-powered services are popular with businesses and consumers.
Microsoft was aggressively early to AI through an investment in OpenAI, but that alliance has frayed. While the software giant has a big business in renting out chips for AI developers through its Azure cloud, its Copilot technology isn't pervasive in the workplace, and its proprietary AI models remain niche.
The company is hosting a Windows and Surface event in San Francisco on Wednesday, describing it in an invitation as "a conversation on how local AI will shape the next chapter of the PC."
Wall Street is lukewarm on the story. Even factoring in a sharp third-quarter rally, the stock is trailing its megacap peers and the broader Nasdaq this year, up just 7% as of Friday's close. Microsoft hasn't beaten the S&P 500 in a calendar year since 2023.
Nasdaq vs. S&P 500 since the end of 2023
Tiffany Wade, co-portfolio manager at Microsoft shareholder Columbia Threadneedle, said there are a lot of unknowns about Copilot, which is the centerpiece of Nadella's AI strategy.
"I think there needs to be a little bit more maturity of the product before we figure out actually what the best solution or what pricing is," Wade said in an interview.
For longtime Microsoft investors, Nadella has a solid track record when it comes to navigating industry shifts. He was named CEO in 2014, succeeding Steve Ballmer, who had presided over a roughly 33% drop in the stock price during his 14-year tenure, as Microsoft slipped into the beleaguered category of legacy software.
Nadella proceeded to turn Microsoft into a cloud powerhouse. He tossed aside perpetual Office software licenses and pushed the company into subscription-based software-as-a-service offerings alongside Azure infrastructure. And he permitted customers to integrate products from bitter rivals like Oracle and Salesforce, rather than insisting on a pure Microsoft stack.
Microsoft's stock price is up roughly 14-fold since Nadella took the helm.
Trained as an electrical engineer and computer scientist, Nadella became a savvy deal-maker, expanding Microsoft through acquisitions of "Minecraft"-maker Mojang, business social network LinkedIn and code-sharing service GitHub.
In recent months, Nadella has acknowledged to investors that he's got to change the business model yet again, this time to reflect the AI-fueled move toward consumption-based pricing. That means becoming a vendor of large volumes of tokens, which measure computing usage and represent the currency of the AI economy.
Success would mean "further expanding our TAM," Nadella said on Microsoft's July earnings call, adopting the acronym for total addressable market.
Microsoft overhauls Copilot to take on AI rivals like Anthropic
Much of the growth story Nadella preaches involves the production of software. Develop more code and do it faster, boosted by the latest and greatest AI tools.
"We went from the code assist to the agentic coding to software factory all within one year," Nadella said at the customer gathering late last month.
Now he wants to see Microsoft clients open their own software factories, spending more along the way to help churn out code. He's also hoping to empower nontechnical knowledge workers. Some of Nadella's lieutenants at the event unveiled a Copilot "super app" that can perform increasingly complex tasks, generate simple applications and function as a virtual teammate.
Nadella had a preview of what was coming.
Microsoft first invested in OpenAI in 2019, when the company was still a fledgling lab. In 2021, a year before ChatGPT launched, Microsoft and OpenAI collaborated to release GitHub Copilot, a tool that could write parts of applications and websites based on vast swaths of public source code.
They'd created an early sensation. But as the generative AI market took off, developers moved to products from AI-native startups like Cursor, now owned by SpaceX, and Anthropic, which rolled out Claude Code.
Microsoft's sluggishness in keeping up with the rapid changes cost GitHub market share.
Earlier this year, Microsoft adjusted the pricing for the coding tool to align more with computing demand. Some customers initially balked, but by July the company said it had racked up 50 million users, up from 26 million last October, meaning that 1 in 5 on GitHub were on board.
Nadella said on the July earnings call that GitHub Copilot sales growth accelerated 60% from the previous quarter, with "significant consumption revenue after the new model went into effect."
"GitHub Copilot went out and learned lessons," said Kyle Daigle, the unit's operating chief, in an interview.
Daigle said GitHub employees shared their lessons with other teams at Microsoft that are eyeing consumption-based pricing schemes.
Hayete Gallot, Microsoft's executive vice president for security products, said the company will charge clients according to how intensely they use the technology.
"I always say to my team, when customers consume, it means we add value. And for me, the truth starts with customers," Gallot said. "If they don't consume, it means we're not giving value."
Currently, Microsoft's enterprise portfolio is reliant on subscriptions. For its core Microsoft 365 productivity suite, which includes Word, Excel and Teams, customers sign up for years at a time, and Copilot costs an extra $30 per person each month. Microsoft has 30 million Copilot seats. The commercial Office 365 base exceeds 450 million.
Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman speaks during an event highlighting Microsoft Copilot, the company's AI tool, on April 4, 2025 in Redmond, Washington. The company also celebrated its 50th anniversary.
Stephen Brashear | Getty Images News | Getty Images
One area of uncertainty in Microsoft's AI road map revolves around Mustafa Suleyman.
Suleyman previously co-founded AI lab DeepMind, which Google bought in 2014. Nadella hired him in 2024 to lead AI initiatives as Microsoft's relationship with OpenAI was cooling.
Last year, Microsoft lost its status as OpenAI's exclusive cloud provider, and this year its license on OpenAI intellectual property became nonexclusive. That left the software company with a massive investment in the AI lab but less preferential treatment. Microsoft said in April that it continues to serve as OpenAI's "primary cloud partner."
Suleyman's group has rolled out models for coding, image generation and reasoning. This week he boasted on X that a new speech-to-text model was "the most accurate real time transcription model in the world... #1 !!!" But for raw digital intellect, the team has yet to rival Anthropic or OpenAI, according to independent leaderboards.
Microsoft executives say there are benefits to having model and application development under the same roof. The group building Teams and other Office productivity apps has seen higher performance from Suleyman's transcription models at a lower price, and engineers get clear feedback as they build out products, said Executive Vice President Charles Lamanna.
"The collaboration is much tighter with Mustafa," he said.
Suleyman maintains a high profile at Microsoft, but his responsibilities have shifted. In March, Microsoft announced that it was bringing together the engineering groups for its commercial and consumer Copilot assistants, as adoption had been sluggish. Jacob Andreou was promoted to executive vice president for Copilot experience, and Suleyman was charged with focusing on model development.
Nadella, meanwhile, has been downplaying the importance of world-beating models in isolation.
"In my view, our priority has to be building a frontier ecosystem, not just a frontier model, so value flows broadly across every company, every industry, and every country," he wrote in a post on his SN Scratchpad website in June.
At the September Copilot event, Nadella stood before a slide declaring that Copilot could connect to "every model," with the Anthropic, OpenAI, SpaceX and Microsoft AI logos.
Increasingly, Microsoft is finding the model leaders encroaching on its turf, as they release products for cybersecurity, customer service and other functions.
In January, as Anthropic's Claude Code was building momentum, Microsoft executives were impressed with its ability to tap a bevy of tools to get things done, said Jared Spataro, Microsoft's marketing chief for AI at work. Microsoft was losing deals to Anthropic, prompting a close study of a rising competitor, said a person familiar with the matter, who asked not to be named due to confidentiality.
A Microsoft spokesperson declined to comment.
Spataro said the company sensed a need to change the mechanics.
"It became very clear to us at that moment. Like, oh wow, the economics are not going to be such that we're going to be able to offer now the best outcome within a fixed price per user per month," Spataro said. "We realized that we needed to start to think about the business model."
The company got cracking on a more comprehensive approach to consumption-based pricing that it calls usage-based billing, or UBB. The first UBB product was Copilot Cowork, which accepts large productivity assignments and shows its progress, Spataro said.
Nadella said on the July earnings call that "earlier this month, we added usage-based billing to Cowork with thousands of customers already paying for and actively using it."
CEO Satya Nadella speaks during Microsoft Build 2026.
Derrick Wood, an analyst at Cowen, said it was a strong signal.
"It may have the effect of what we saw when Claude Code, for example, shifted to consumption pricing, and you saw token bills go significantly higher," said Wood, who recommends buying Microsoft shares. "There's definitely the possibility for that to happen with Cowork."
Nadella is a user. On a podcast recorded after the September event, he said he can ask Cowork to prepare a supply chain optimization spreadsheet showing multiple scenarios.
"It'll create a fantastic artifact," he said.

Microsoft (MSFT) Stock Rises as Oppenheimer Raises Price Target on Copilot Overhaul
Microsoft (MSFT) stock rose 4% after Oppenheimer raised its price target to $570 following a major Copilot enterprise overhaul.
By Trader EdgeSeptember 26, 20264 Mins Read
Microsoft stock rose as much as 4% on Friday, hitting $516.39 in afternoon trading.
Oppenheimer analyst Brian Schwartz raised his MSFT price target to $570 from $515, keeping an Outperform rating.
Microsoft merged its consumer and workplace Copilot assistants into one enterprise-focused app.
The new app is built around three tools: a home chat hub, a coding tool, and an agent called Autopilot.
Microsoft stock is up 7% year to date, well behind the Technology Select Sector SPDR Fund’s 37% gain.
Microsoft stock climbed on Friday, rising as much as 4% to reach $516.39 in afternoon trading. The move came after Oppenheimer raised its price target on the tech giant and Microsoft rolled out a major overhaul of its Copilot app.
Oppenheimer analyst Brian Schwartz lifted his price target on Microsoft to $570 from $515. He kept his Outperform rating in place. Schwartz pointed to customers increasingly standardizing on Microsoft as their main enterprise AI platform.
Stifel analyst Brad Reback also raised his outlook. He upgraded Microsoft from hold to buy and pushed his price target up to $575 from $530. That target points to roughly 11% upside from Friday’s closing price.
Technology stocks broadly helped lift the market on Friday. The Technology Select Sector SPDR Fund, which holds Microsoft as one of its largest positions, rose 0.8%. The S&P 500 was up a smaller 0.2%.
Microsoft merged its consumer and workplace Copilot assistants into a single app built for businesses. That move ends the company’s push to build a personal AI companion for everyday users.
Microsoft executive Charles Lamanna explained the thinking at a preview event. He said the company isn’t trying to build a personal companion app, and instead wants to help people get work done.
The redesigned app centers on three tools. A home hub combines chat with task delegation, letting users edit Word, Excel, and PowerPoint files directly inside the app.
A second tool, built on GitHub Copilot technology, lets non-technical staff build apps and workflows using plain language. It runs inside a sandbox that a company’s IT team controls.
The third tool, called Autopilot, acts as a persistent agent living inside a company’s own cloud setup. It can handle multi-step background tasks without constant human input.
Microsoft’s pricing now follows a split model. Everyday chat use comes with a fixed subscription fee, while longer agentic tasks get billed on a pay-as-you-go basis.
This shift changes how predictable Microsoft’s AI revenue will be. The company has more than 30 million paid Copilot enterprise subscriptions, which gave it a steady, seat-based revenue base.
Usage-based billing ties part of that revenue to how often customers actually run the agent tools. That’s a different setup than counting fixed seats each month.
Not everyone gets Microsoft’s full attention here. Alphabet continues targeting consumer AI users through Gemini, and OpenAI does the same with ChatGPT. Alphabet stock was up 0.68% to $344.70 on Friday.
Microsoft stock has lagged its own sector for most of 2026. Shares are up 7% year to date, compared to a 37% gain for the Technology Select Sector SPDR Fund over the same stretch.
Schwartz flagged some risks alongside his price target increase. He pointed to AI disruption and the possibility that companies pull forward their enterprise tech spending, both of which could weigh on Microsoft’s growth path.
Microsoft’s stock carries a Buy consensus among 55 analysts covering the company, with 14 rating it Strong Buy and 38 rating it Buy. Three analysts rate it Hold.
Microsoft closed Thursday at $497.93 before Friday’s rally. The stock’s 52-week range spans from $348.54 to $549.20.

Microsoft OneDrive to Drop Support for These iPhone Models - MacRumors
Microsoft OneDrive to Drop Support for These iPhone Models
Tuesday October 6, 2026 4:53 am PDT by Tim Hardwick
Microsoft is set to drop OneDrive support for iOS 18 and iPadOS 18, which will remove the cloud storage app's compatibility with several older iPhones and one iPad model.
The loss of support for iOS 18 will impact the iPhone XR, iPhone XS, and iPhone XS Max, because these devices can't be updated to iOS 26. Likewise, the seventh-generation iPad will be left behind when Microsoft raises the app's minimum requirement to iPadOS 26.
OneDrive 18.12.1 is the final version to support iOS 18 and iPadOS 18, based on release notes for Microsoft's latest TestFlight beta.
It's not clear when the change will translate to the public version of OneDrive. That said, Microsoft recently added a notice to its App Store listing saying that support for iOS and iPadOS 18 will be dropped "soon," and recommending that users update to iOS 26 or iOS 27 to continue receiving the latest versions.
Existing versions of OneDrive aren't expected to immediately stop working on affected devices, but they won't receive new features, fixes, or other app updates once Microsoft makes the change.

pages.title: I replaced Microsoft 365 with free open-source apps, but this one app is hard to leave behind
pages.text:
Beginning his professional journey in the tech industry in 2018, Yash spent over three years as a Software Engineer. After that, he shifted his focus to empowering readers through informative and engaging content on his tech blog – DiGiTAL BiRYANi. He has also published tech articles for MakeTechEasier. He loves to explore new tech gadgets and platforms. When he is not writing, you’ll find him exploring food. He is known as Digital Chef Yash among his readers because of his love for Technology and Food.
I’ve used Microsoft 365 for years, so moving away from it felt like a bigger experiment than simply uninstalling a few apps. I wanted to see how far I could go with free, open-source software without making my daily workflow harder. Instead of looking for one package to replace everything, I tested different tools for different jobs and used them long enough to see where they actually fit. Everything worked more smoothly than I expected, but one part of the experience made me realize just how much I had taken a certain Microsoft app for granted.
LibreOffice is the first replacement that really makes me question whether I need Microsoft 365 at all. When I started using it, I expected plenty of compromises, but most never became a problem in my daily work.
Writer handles the documents I create regularly, and I don't have to change much about how I work. Calc gives me everything I need for the spreadsheets I actually use, while Impress works well for the occasional presentation. The interface feels familiar enough that I can open any of the apps and get started without spending time learning a new workflow.
I did notice some differences when working with Microsoft Office files, especially with formatting, but they haven't been enough to make me switch back. LibreOffice continues to handle my everyday office work without a subscription, and it has become a perfectly practical replacement.
Nextcloud is another replacement that fits into my workflow without requiring much adjustment. I mainly use it to keep my files available across devices, much like I did with OneDrive. Once I had it set up, I could access the same folders from my desktop, browser, and other devices whenever I needed them.
What I like most is that my files are no longer tied to Microsoft's cloud. I decide where the data is stored, how much space I want, and which folders I want to sync. The desktop client also keeps the experience familiar because files appear directly in my file manager instead of forcing me to manage everything through a browser.
It isn't completely maintenance-free, though. Since I'm running Nextcloud myself, updates, storage, backups, and occasional troubleshooting are now my responsibility. Still, that trade-off works for me. Nextcloud gives me the cloud storage experience I need while giving me much more control over where my files actually live.
Joplin turned out to be one of the easiest Microsoft 365 replacements for me. I mainly wanted a simple place to write, organize, and find my notes, and Joplin covers those needs without making things unnecessarily complicated.
I organize my notes into notebooks, add tags when needed, and can quickly search through everything when I need to find something. The editor also feels comfortable for everyday writing, so I didn't have to completely change how I take notes. I especially like that Joplin uses Markdown, which keeps my notes portable instead of locking them into a proprietary format.
Another thing I appreciate is how flexible the app feels. I can use it across my devices and keep my notes organized in a way that makes sense to me. It doesn't try to turn note-taking into a huge productivity system, which I actually prefer.
After using Joplin for a while, I stopped thinking about what I was missing from OneNote. For my note-taking needs, it simply works.
Half-baked new Outlook made me switch to Thunderbird
New Outlook is where my Microsoft 365 replacement experiment takes an unexpected turn. I had already moved away from Microsoft's other apps, but I still wanted a dependable email client. Unfortunately, the new Outlook experience doesn't feel like the Outlook I was used to.
Some of the changes felt unnecessary, and I found myself spending more time adjusting to the new interface instead of simply managing my email. It also feels less like the complete desktop email client I had relied on for years. That was enough to make me look elsewhere.
Thunderbird became the obvious option because I wanted something straightforward and open source. After installing it, I connected my email accounts and got back to basics without dealing with Microsoft's ecosystem. The interface isn't identical to Outlook, but that's not really the point for me. I want an email client that stays out of my way and gives me control over how I manage my inbox. Thunderbird isn't perfect, but it fits my current workflow better.
After replacing almost every part of Microsoft 365, Outlook is the one app I still genuinely miss. Classic Outlook wasn't perfect, but it was fast, capable, and felt like a proper desktop application. I only realized how much I valued that after switching away from it.
What frustrates me is that Microsoft already had something that worked. Instead of improving the experience I liked, the new Outlook feels slower, more bloated, and increasingly focused on features I don't really need.
Thunderbird works well enough for me, and I don't regret moving away from Microsoft 365. But I still hope Microsoft remembers what made Classic Outlook so good. I don't need more AI features or another redesign. I just want Outlook to feel fast, stable, and useful again. That's the version I'd happily come back to.

pages.title: A Teachers Union and Microsoft Just Made An AI Safety Deal. But Compliance Remains an Open Question. – Mother Jones
pages.text:
Randi Weingarten, president of the American Federation of Teachers, speaks during a protest against budget cuts initiated by President Trump and DOGE in Washington, D.C. on March 13, 2025.Bryan Dozier / Middle East Images / Middle East Images/AFP/Getty
Get your news from a source that’s not owned and controlled by oligarchs. Sign up for the free Mother Jones Daily.
On Wednesday morning, in a Manhattan press room containing about 50 reporters and union members, one of the largest teachers’ unions in the US announced an agreement with Microsoft that, among other things, prohibits the tech company from tracking student use of its AI tools and applying student and teacher data to train AI models.
The guidelines listed in the American Federation of Teachers’ deal with Microsoft apply to any school district “that desires the same principles” when forming their own customer agreements with the company and purchasing its AI products.
The union also gives Microsoft—and any other tech company that signs on (AFT President Randi Weingarten mentioned ongoing conversations with OpenAI and Anthropic during Wednesday’s announcement)—a 180-day deadline to delete records of AI data use from students and school districts on its active systems following a request.
Microsoft agreed not to use student and teacher data to train its AI — but there are exceptions. The guidelines point out “narrow safety and security” situations, including letting the company use “the minimum amount” of school user data to detect, prevent, investigate, or remediate harm to users or security threats to its AI products and retain it “for as long as reasonably necessary.”
The contract also lists “contractual remedies” for school districts that sign on, such as the ability to pause or discontinue Microsoft’s deployment of its AI systems if the company commits any material breaches of its agreement obligations.
The current guidelines do not present explicit, quantifiable rules for what is considered remediation by a “reasonable” time—it’s something that both Microsoft and the customer will “engage in good faith” to come up with.
When I asked Microsoft Vice Chair and President Brad Smith about specific guidelines on how an accountability process will work if Microsoft fails to comply with remediation on Wednesday, he largely dodged the question, saying that Microsoft has to publish reports that provide transparency to the AFT and school districts and have tight deadlines for fixes.
“Obviously, this [remediation process] becomes part of our broader contract with each school district, and all of those [existing] contracts already have built-in remedies,” Smith told Mother Jones. “I think that there’s just an unprecedented amount of transparency associated with the commitments that are in this agreement.”
When I asked again about specific steps that will be taken if Microsoft fails to comply, Smith said they are “connected back into the provisions that we have in our contract with each school district. Those can vary.”
“Mostly, what I find is that what people want when something goes wrong is just to go fix it. People don’t want to end up with more time with lawyers,” he continued. “That’s always an option if somebody wants to take action, but let’s just fix problems when they arise.”
While accountability applies to how each school district will work with Microsoft in the near future, the company seemingly not holding discussions now raises questions about the feasibility of contract enforceability.
Microsoft, and other companies like Google, have a history of promoting their AI products to schools and educators, and a healthy skepticism is needed when relying in part on tech companies to police AI and previous failures of implementing educational technology.
Weingarten and Michael Mulgrew, president of the United Federation of Teachers representing New York City public school educators and others, who were also taking questions immediately following the announcement, did not respond to the question.
The contract comes a week after New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced a one-year moratorium on AI use for elementary and middle school students in the city’s public schools, and the Los Angeles Unified School District announced restrictions to generative AI platforms for all students for the 2026-27 school year.
The AFT’s contract with Microsoft contains the sentence “When in doubt, protect the student.” on the bottom of each of the 31 pages. But exactly how any of these policies around AI use in schools will actually work remains unclear.

pages.title: Meta and Microsoft want to stop their employees using Claude
pages.text:
Skip to navigation Skip to main content Skip to right column
Meta and Microsoft want to stop their employees using Claude
Tue, October 6, 2026 at 6:10 AM PDT 2 min read
When you buy through links on our articles, Future and its syndication partners may earn a commission.
Meta halved its number of Claude seats while pushing MetaCode adoption
Microsoft also reportedly asked workers to use Copilot over Claude
Anthropic could face reputational damage from DoD designation
There seems to be an ongoing shift away from Claude happening in Big Tech, but the reasons behind why two major companies are looking to reduce Claude expenditure aren't so clear.
Cost could be one of the biggest factors, with Microsoft's internal Claude spending estimated to have been on course for at least $1 billion this year, per The Information.
With both Microsoft and Meta having their own internal AI systems, it makes sense for them both to use their own tools for less cash.
Meta and Microsoft reportedly cutting down on Claude usage
Microsoft had already asked employees to limit their Claude usage and spend more time with Copilot and other Microsoft tools, The Information shared, while Meta has reportedly halved the number of its workers using Claude Code from 60,000 earlier this year to just 30,000. At the same time, its internal alternative, MetaCode, has already passed 30,000 users.
Meta, too, was set to spend billions on internal AI usage before the company imposed token limits, spending controls and other monitoring.
We've already seen similar trends among smaller AI customers, with US organizations opting for cheaper Chinese models over homegrown alternatives. It's likely an important economic equation, where paying significantly less for a marginally interior model becomes the most viable option for most use cases.
Anthropic itself has also had a troubling couple of months, after being deemed a national security supply chain risk by the US Department of Defense. A designation that will have undoubtedly altered consumer and enterprise perception of the company, irrespective of the designation's potentially political founding.
"The company may experience material revenue losses or business disruptions attributable to these events," Anthropic warned in an IPO prospectus (via Reuters).
The bigger story impacts Anthropic – potentially losing billions in revenue from two of its biggest customers could seriously impact revenue for a company that's slated to go public for a reported valuation of over $2 trillion (per Reuters).

AMD and Microsoft Haven’t Undertaken Stock Splits for 20+ Years And Investors Shouldn’t Care
AMD's data center business exploded while Microsoft rents the very racks AMD fills, yet one of these stocks looks dangerously priced for anything less than a perfect Helios launch. Here is what actually separates the safer AI bet from the…
Published October 6, 2026, 7:15am ET · 2 min read
This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them.
A crucial AI chip sits at the heart of a circuit board, symbolizing the core technology driving the artificial intelligence industry and shaping investment decisions for companies like Nvidia and Broadcom. © Quality Stock Arts / Shutterstock.com
Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ:AMD | AMD Price Prediction) and Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) last split their shares in 2000 and 2003. Both just reported quarters where AI demand outran supply. AMD sells the chips; Microsoft rents the compute and sells the software. Those businesses matter far more to returns than share count.
Both Stocks Soared Over Ten Years Without a Split
A split cuts each share into smaller pieces without changing the company’s value. Over ten years, AMD rose 9259.26% and Microsoft gained 923.23% with no splits. Fractional share trading means a high share price rarely keeps small investors out.
Data Center Doubles at AMD While Azure Grows 43%
AMD’s revenue rose 50.1% to $11.54 billion. Data Center sales jumped 107% and now make up 58% of revenue. Lisa Su said “customer demand for Venice is stronger than for any prior EPYC generation.” Gaming fell 31%.
Microsoft’s revenue rose 17.8% to $90.01 billion, and Azure grew 43%. Copilot passed 30 million paid seats. Commercial backlog reached $678 billion but grew only 25% excluding OpenAI. CFO Amy Hood said “demand continues to exceed available supply.”
AMD Supplies the Racks Microsoft Is Buying
The two companies do business with each other. Microsoft “will deploy Helios at scale on Azure,” AMD said. Microsoft also makes its own chips and runs NVIDIA (NASDAQ:NVDA) hardware, and Satya Nadella stressed that “any given model at any given time is swappable.” Being able to switch suppliers gives Microsoft pricing leverage over vendors like AMD. Microsoft expects capital spending of about $175 billion in fiscal 2027, and much of that money becomes revenue for chipmakers, along with the power, cooling, and networking suppliers we profiled in a free report on seven AI infrastructure names outside the chip aisle.
Helios Shipments Will Decide Who Pulls Ahead
AMD guided third-quarter revenue to about $13 billion. Su said Helios shipments start in Q3 and step up in Q4. Yields on that rack bear watching, since Su admitted the product is “highly complex.” For Microsoft, keep an eye on whether Azure hits its guided 45% growth while all those new data centers come online.
Why Microsoft Offers Steadier AI Exposure
AMD gained 283.65% over the past year, while Microsoft rose 2.35%. After a run like that, AMD’s valuation leaves little room for a delayed Helios ramp. Microsoft offers a lower multiple and the breadth of a platform that benefits whichever chip wins. AMD’s order book from OpenAI, Meta Platforms (NASDAQ:META) and Anthropic gives it the stronger growth profile, along with sharper swings. My view could shift if Microsoft’s growth outside OpenAI slows. Neither company’s split history moves my view either way.

Microsoft or Alphabet: If I Could Only Own 1 AI Giant Until Retirement, This Is It
Alphabet just posted 40% gains and trades at a cheaper multiple, so why does one analyst still reach for Microsoft when building a retirement position that has to last decades?
Published October 6, 2026, 8:00am ET · 3 min read
This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them.
This graphic depicts the financial showdown between Microsoft and Alphabet, illustrating which AI giant might better secure a long-term investment for retirement. © 24/7 Wall St.
Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT | MSFT Price Prediction) orAlphabet (NASDAQ:GOOGL): If you could buy only one AI giant for your account and hold it for decades, which one belongs there right now? I pick Microsoft. Alphabet has the stronger recent momentum, and Microsoft still wins on durability.
Alphabet’s Strongest Case, and Why It Falls Short
Alphabet’s bull case is a strong one. Its shares gained 40.91% over the past year, compared with 2.7% for Microsoft. Alphabet changes hands at 15 times trailing earnings, while Microsoft trades at 29. Google Cloud revenue jumped 82% to $24.77 billion in the second quarter.
That cheap multiple is inflated by a one-time item, though. Alphabet’s Q2 EPS of $9.11 included a $99.03 billion unrealized gain on equity securities. On forward earnings the gap mostly closes: 23x for Alphabet versus 25x for Microsoft. So valuation gives Alphabet only a slight edge, and the three dimensions that matter most for a retirement holding all go to Microsoft.
Cloud and AI Monetization: Microsoft’s Backlog Wins
Google Cloud is growing faster, with a backlog of more than $460 billion as of Q1. Microsoft’s contracted revenue is larger. Commercial remaining performance obligations (signed contracts not yet billed) rose 84% to $678 billion. Azure topped $100 billion in annual revenue for the first time, grew 43% in fiscal Q4, and is guided to about 45% growth in constant currency next quarter. Microsoft 365 Copilot has more than 30 million paid seats.
Retirees should care most about how widely that revenue is spread. Nearly 90% of full-year Microsoft Cloud revenue came from customers outside frontier-model companies.
Cash Generation and Shareholder Returns: Alphabet Pulled Back
Both companies are spending heavily on AI. Microsoft’s fiscal 2026 capex reached $115.95 billion, and free cash flow slipped 6.5% to $66.99 billion. Management guided to roughly $175 billion of fiscal 2027 capex and still expects to stay free-cash-flow positive. Microsoft also returned more than $43 billion to shareholders during the year.
Alphabet’s free cash flow turned negative in Q2, at -$5.86 billion. The company raised about $70 billion in combined equity and debt, long-term debt grew from $46.5 billion to $98.2 billion, and it suspended its buyback. Microsoft also has the higher dividend yield, at 0.69% versus 0.5%.
Regulatory and Competitive Exposure: Search Is the Weak Spot
Search still drives Alphabet’s profits, bringing in $63.27 billion in Q2. A court order requiring Google to share data and syndicate search results to rivals took effect after a judge denied Google’s request for a stay. Federal regulators have also told an appeals court the remedies are too weak. On top of that, AI chatbots now compete directly for search queries.
Microsoft’s main exposure is OpenAI, in which it holds a stake of roughly 27%. Even without OpenAI, its backlog grew 25%. Barron’s upgraded the stock on Monday and called Microsoft the “adult in charge” on AI security.
Verdict: Microsoft Is the More Durable Retirement Holding
Microsoft is my pick. Its operating margin is 46.8%, compared with 32.1% at Alphabet, and its interest coverage is 50.9x. Over 10 years it has returned 933.55%, versus 768.46% for Alphabet. Its beta, a measure of how much a stock swings relative to the market, is 1.108, compared with 1.225 for Alphabet. Alphabet suits growth investors who are comfortable with volatility. Microsoft is the stock you can own without checking it every day.
Here is what would break that thesis: AI demand cools while capex keeps climbing. If fiscal 2027 free cash flow turns negative despite management’s guidance, or if operating margins fall by more than the less than one point decline Microsoft has guided to, the durability argument weakens. The company insists it can slow GPU purchases if demand shifts. The next earnings report will be the first test of that promise.

Microsoft’s AI Investment Could Pay Off for Years. Here’s My Price Target
Azure just crossed a milestone that most analysts dismissed as years away, and Microsoft's backlog tells a story the stock price has not caught up to yet.
Published September 27, 2026, 11:30am ET · 3 min read
Price Targets desk. Editor: Vandita Jadeja.
This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them.
Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella discusses the company's pioneering AI strategy. His recent essay, "The Reverse Information Paradox," outlines a new direction for enterprise AI adoption.
Our Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT | MSFT Price Prediction) call is straightforward: the AI investment cycle is starting to produce real financial leverage, and the market has not fully repriced it.
The 24/7 Wall St. price target for Microsoft is $613.43, versus a current price of $495.22. That implies 22.85% upside over the next 12 months. Our recommendation is buy, and our confidence level is high at 90%.
24/7 Wall St. Price Target Summary for MSFT
Microsoft is roughly flat over the past year at -1.95%, but shorter-term momentum has quietly returned: up 1.62% in the past month and 3.05% year to date.
The bigger story is fundamentals. Fiscal Q4 2026 revenue hit $90.01 billion, up 17.8% year over year, non-GAAP EPS of $4.74 beat estimates by 11.81%, and Azure crossed $100 billion in full-year revenue for the first time. Even a previously skeptical analyst at CNBC this week said Microsoft has “clearly turned the corner” on monetizing its buildout.
The bull case rests on the RPO backlog. Commercial remaining performance obligations surged 84% year over year to $678 billion, giving Microsoft multi-year revenue visibility few software companies can match.
Azure grew 43%, Microsoft 365 Copilot passed 30 million paid seats, and CFO Amy Hood told investors that “demand continues to exceed available supply” for Azure capacity.
If the FY27 Azure guide of roughly 45% growth in constant currency holds, our bull-case one-year path reaches $710.57. The Wall Street consensus target of $576.40 sits between our base and bull scenarios.
The bear case starts with capex. Full-year FY26 capital expenditures ballooned to $115.95 billion, dragging free cash flow down 6.46% despite record earnings. OpenAI-related investment losses widened to $3.1 billion in Q1 FY26.
That said, bulls would argue this reflects investment in future capacity: the $678 billion RPO covers the buildout, and Hood emphasized that GPU-heavy capex is “short-lived assets” that can be throttled if demand softens.
All of that spending has to be powered, cooled, and networked by somebody, and we pulled together seven companies doing exactly that in a free AI infrastructure report. Our bear-case one-year path still lands at $523.51, above today’s price.
How Microsoft Compares to Alphabet and Amazon
Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOGL) is the sharpest valuation contrast. Google Cloud grew 82% in Q2 2026, faster than Azure, yet Alphabet trades at a trailing P/E of just 15 versus Microsoft’s 28. That makes Microsoft look expensive on the multiple, but its 46.78% operating margin dwarfs Alphabet’s 34%.
Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN) is the direct hyperscaler comparison. AWS revenue grew 37% in Q2 2026 at a 39.4% AWS operating margin, but Amazon’s overall net margin is only 10.83% versus Microsoft’s 40.31%. On a per-dollar-of-earnings basis, our $613.43 target for Microsoft looks reasonable on the earnings power.
The 24/7 Wall St. price target for Microsoft is $613.43, a buy rating with 90% confidence. The key factor tipping the scale is the $678 billion RPO backlog, which converts today’s capex into tomorrow’s revenue.
The bullish case strengthens if Azure holds its mid-40s growth rate into calendar 2027. The thesis weakens if AI capex growth outpaces RPO conversion for two consecutive quarters. On balance, the setup favors the bull scenario.
These projections assume Microsoft continues executing on Azure and Copilot monetization. Significant upside or downside could result from AI infrastructure returns, OpenAI partnership economics, or a broader tech multiple reset.

Our bear case comes to at $533.45. Q4 capital spending rose 109.63% to $35.80 billion, and free cash flow fell 23.19%. Management expects fiscal 2027 capex of about $175 billion. More Personal Computing, which includes Windows and Xbox, contracted 4%. Excluding OpenAI, backlog grew a more modest 25%.
Operating cash flow rose 30% to $55.44 billion, and Microsoft expects free cash flow to stay positive. Hood said spending is flexible: "If the demand environment changes, you just slow down what is, in fact, the largest component."

Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOGL) trades at 15x earnings, and Google Cloud grew 82%. A $99.03 billion gain on equity securities inflated those earnings. Alphabet had negative Q2 free cash flow of $5.855 billion and suspended its buyback.
Against these peers, our target looks reasonable. Microsoft has premium-quality cash flow at a valuation between the two.
I stand by our 24/7 Wall St. price target of $627.63, a buy rating and 90% confidence. Capacity selling as soon as it arrives tips the scale. My confidence would rise if Azure delivers the guided acceleration and Copilot seat additions keep compounding.
I would get more conservative if capex keeps growing while free cash flow contracted for several more quarters. For now, the evidence supports the bull side.

We thought Microsoft was preparing a wild laptop. Turns out it's preparing two.
The Surface Laptop Ultra may bring a new class of machine to the Windows space. © Kyle Barr / Gizmodo
At this point, the writing has been on the wall for Microsoft’s Surface Laptop Ultra for some time. The company has been parading the thing around all summer, heralding its AI capabilities and demonstrating its capacity to chew through demanding games with admirable ease. We’ve known since Computex that the Ultra would be among a whole laundry list of laptops rolling out this year powered by Nvidia’s new RTX Spark, an Apple-style superchip that staples a CPU, GPU, and unified memory together. And that, along with Microsoft’s not-at-all-subtle marketing, made it fairly evident that the Surface Laptop Ultra was being positioned as an AI machine.
Here’s where things get interesting. The RTX Spark platform has two variants: one with 18 cores and one with 20. We predicted back at IFA that many laptops would contain the 18-core chip, given that that’s, you know, the one that seems more evidently useful for laptops and that Nvidia was demoing the 20-core version in mini PCs at the same show.
But the Surface Laptop Ultra, it turns out, is not trying to be an ordinary laptop. Windows Central’s Zac Bowden has leaked nearly all remaining details of Microsoft’s upcoming MacBook Pro competitor, and one of them is very spicy. Per the leaks, Microsoft will be selling the Ultra with both RTX Spark variants, including that 20-core monstrosity that we all kind of figured we’d only see crammed into weird-looking mini PCs.
Microsoft’s eighteener reportedly maxes out at 32GB of memory; the 20-core guy goes all the way up to 128GB. Also of note: the entry-level 18-core SKUs will reportedly run Windows 11 Home, while higher-end configs get Windows 11 Pro. The tangible difference between these operating systems is mainly security and virtualization stuff, but the signaling here is important—the 20-core option is targeting a very different market segment.
The Surface Laptop (above) could be morphing into a laptop that rivals the most powerful MacBook Pro. © Kyle Barr / Gizmodo
This is interesting for a few reasons. The fact that Microsoft is positioning this Ultra device as a rival to Apple’s M5 Max MacBook Pro is no secret (I mean, look at the thing). What I didn’t necessarily expect was that Redmond planned on spanning the whole gamut, from the 24GB entry-level notebook all the way up the chain.
Bowden’s sources say that the upcoming event will focus on “how Surface Laptop Ultra and RTX Spark are capable of running local 120B parameter models that enable on-device AI experiences and agentic workflows,” and that the company plans to “demonstrate how the Surface Laptop Ultra maintains maximum performance even when not plugged in.” These both appear to be direct attacks on what Apple’s most premium systems are traditionally known for in this space: maintaining high performance on battery and enabling large local AI workloads to dive headfirst into a massive pool of memory.
Previously, there was a real question as to whether Microsoft was building one several-thousand-dollar halo product tailored to folks who know what “120B parameter model” means or a broader product family. Now, we at least know that there are two clear tiers. Microsoft has one horse in the premium consumer laptop race and another that’s just hoping to take a big bite out of the customer base Apple’s arguably had cornered since the launch of the M-series. It’s shoving the maximum possible performance into a machine with a 2,000-nit-peak-HDR screen and hoping for the best.
Of course, this whole equation is missing one major variable: cost. Bowden’s sources have not confirmed an exact price, and that number will definitively determine where this 20-core Ultra model fits in the current market. I’m willing to make a bold prediction, though: it probably won’t be cheap.
